quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Values, Variables, and Control Flow
quizzes.intro: Check types, declarations, equality, and basic decision-making before functions and arrays.

questions.prompt: Which declaration should you prefer by default for a binding you will not reassign?
questions.explanation: const documents non-reassignment intent and is the modern default when the binding stays fixed.

wrongExplanations.a: var is legacy, function-scoped, and easier to misuse.
wrongExplanations.c: static is not how ordinary local bindings are declared in beginner JS.
wrongExplanations.d: define is not a JavaScript variable keyword.

questions.prompt: Why is === usually preferred over == for comparisons?

options.text: Because === is slower and therefore safer
Because === avoids the surprising type coercion that == can perform

questions.explanation: Strict equality compares without the loose coercion rules that confuse beginners.

wrongExplanations.a: Preference is about clarity and correctness, not slowness.
wrongExplanations.c: == can compare numbers, but may coerce other types unexpectedly.
wrongExplanations.d: === works across comparable types without coercion.

options.text: A value was intentionally cleared with a special empty object
A binding has been declared but not assigned a value yet, or a missing property/result
The value is exactly equal to false

questions.explanation: undefined commonly means no value has been assigned or returned yet.

wrongExplanations.a: Intentional emptiness is often expressed with null by convention.
wrongExplanations.c: undefined is a value, not automatically a crash.
wrongExplanations.d: undefined is falsy but not the boolean false.

questions.prompt: Which value is falsy in a conditional?
questions.explanation: An empty string is falsy; empty arrays/objects and the string "0" are truthy.

wrongExplanations.a: Empty arrays are truthy in JavaScript conditionals.

questions.prompt: What is the result of "2" + 2 in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: The + operator concatenates when one operand is a string, producing "22".

wrongExplanations.a: Numeric addition does not happen when a string triggers concatenation.
wrongExplanations.c: NaN appears in invalid numeric operations, not this concatenation.
wrongExplanations.d: This expression returns a string, not a boolean.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Functions, Arrays, and Objects
quizzes.intro: Test reusable functions and collection transformations.

options.text: Deletes every element that fails a test
Creates a new array by transforming each element
Sorts an array in place only
Converts an object into JSON text

questions.explanation: map returns a new array with the results of calling a function on every item.

wrongExplanations.a: Filtering is the job of filter, not map.
wrongExplanations.c: sort handles ordering and mutates the array; map transforms values.
wrongExplanations.d: JSON.stringify converts values to JSON text.

questions.prompt: If const a = { score: 1 }; const b = a; b.score = 2; what is a.score?

options.text: 1, because objects are always copied on assignment
2, because a and b reference the same object

questions.explanation: Object assignment copies the reference, so mutating through b also changes a.

wrongExplanations.a: Assignment does not deep-copy objects by default.
wrongExplanations.c: score remains a defined number property.
wrongExplanations.d: The value is still a number, not a string.

questions.prompt: Which statement about arrow functions is most accurate for beginners?

options.text: They are the only valid function syntax in JavaScript
They provide concise syntax and are commonly used for short callbacks

questions.explanation: Arrow functions are a compact form frequently used for callbacks and small helpers.

wrongExplanations.a: Traditional function declarations remain fully valid.
wrongExplanations.c: Arrow functions can return values, including via implicit return.
wrongExplanations.d: Await still requires async functions and explicit await.

options.text: A single boolean summarizing the whole array
A new array containing elements that pass the test function
The original array mutated in place

questions.explanation: filter keeps items for which the callback returns a truthy value and returns a new array.

wrongExplanations.a: some/every return booleans; filter returns an array.
wrongExplanations.d: filter does not mutate the source array.

options.text: Deleting object keys permanently from disk
Extracting values from objects or arrays into named variables cleanly

questions.explanation: Destructuring unpacks properties or array positions into variables with concise syntax.

wrongExplanations.a: Destructuring reads values; it is not a disk-deletion tool.
wrongExplanations.c: TypeScript compilation is separate from destructuring syntax.
wrongExplanations.d: Destructuring has no special power over async control flow.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — DOM, Async, and Judgment
quizzes.intro: Apply essentials to interaction, asynchronous work, and debugging judgment.

questions.prompt: Why prefer textContent over innerHTML when inserting plain text?

options.text: Because textContent is the only property that can change the DOM
Because textContent avoids interpreting markup, which is safer for plain text
Because innerHTML cannot update visible text

questions.explanation: textContent sets text without parsing HTML, reducing injection risk for untrusted strings.

wrongExplanations.a: Many APIs can update the DOM.
wrongExplanations.c: innerHTML can update content, but parses HTML.

questions.prompt: What happens if you forget await on an async function call that returns a Promise?

options.text: You receive a Promise object instead of the resolved value
The program converts it into a string automatically

questions.explanation: Without await (or then), you work with the Promise itself, not the eventual result.

wrongExplanations.a: Forgetting await does not pause execution for the result.
wrongExplanations.d: No automatic string conversion of the resolved payload occurs.

questions.prompt: Which habit best improves debuggability of beginner JavaScript?

options.text: Write one giant function that does everything
Keep small functions, inspect values at key points, and test with tiny fixtures

questions.explanation: Small units and deliberate inspection make wrong assumptions easier to find.

wrongExplanations.c: Error messages and stack traces are primary clues.

questions.prompt: What does optional chaining (?.) help with?

options.text: Forcing every missing property to throw immediately
Safely accessing nested properties that may be null or undefined

questions.explanation: Optional chaining short-circuits to undefined when it hits nullish intermediate values.

wrongExplanations.a: It reduces throw risk on missing chains rather than forcing throws.
wrongExplanations.c: DOM creation uses other APIs such as createElement.
wrongExplanations.d: Sorting is unrelated to optional chaining.

questions.prompt: Which check correctly detects an empty array for control flow?
questions.explanation: Empty arrays are truthy, so check length explicitly.

wrongExplanations.a: An empty array is truthy, so !items is false.
wrongExplanations.c: empty is not a special JS keyword for this comparison.
wrongExplanations.d: A single equals assigns, and it is not an emptiness test.

questions.prompt: A function runs without throwing, but the UI shows the wrong total. What does that guarantee?

options.text: Only that the code executed—logic, data shape, or assumptions may still be wrong

questions.explanation: Successful execution is not proof of correct results; verify data and logic separately.

wrongExplanations.a: Wrong logic can still run cleanly.
wrongExplanations.c: Missing awaits can still produce wrong UI without immediate throws.
wrongExplanations.d: Mutation issues can exist without exceptions.
